brief: BofA, a longtime bond bear, argues the 10-year Treasury yield near 5% has moved above the S&P 500's trailing earnings yield and widened its gap versus the dividend yield to about 4 points, near 2000s highs, so bonds are starting to compete with equities for capital rather than just influencing them. BofA's 5/6/7 framework: at 5% investors become indifferent between bonds and stocks; above 6% higher yields have coincided with weaker equity returns; above 7% valuation damage from multiple compression becomes clear. Markets are currently in the 5% bucket, where the S&P has historically still averaged 0.8% monthly returns when yields rose, falling to near zero at 6-7% and turning negative above 7%, so 5% is competition, not destruction yet. Why yields rise matters: growth-driven increases differ from inflation or sovereign-risk-driven ones, and MOVE outrunning equity vol signals the repricing path is violent. BofA's valuation model implies roughly -3% annualized S&P price returns over a decade versus +3% equal-weighted, on 20.4x forward earnings. Large-cap balance sheets are largely insulated (80% long-term fixed debt, sub-1% EPS hit through 2028), but small caps carry 40%+ short-term or floating debt, and government net interest expense is at a record share of GDP.
